title: Halicin: a deep-learning-identified antibiotic validated in vitro and in mice, with no verified human outcome
summary: A deep-learning screen identified halicin, active in vitro and in mice and confirmed by other labs; no human outcome.
account: Jonathan Stokes, Regina Barzilay, James Collins and colleagues at MIT, the Broad Institute, Harvard and McMaster University published in Cell on 20 February 2020. They reported halicin, a molecule identified by a directed-message-passing neural network trained on 2,335 molecules to predict inhibition of E. coli growth. Halicin, originally investigated as a kinase inhibitor for diabetes, is structurally divergent from conventional antibiotics. It reduced Acinetobacter baumannii in a mouse wound model and cleared Clostridioides difficile in a mouse infection model. Independent laboratories at KACST in Riyadh (December 2021) and Central South University in Changsha (September 2022) confirmed antibacterial activity in vitro. The latter also in a mouse abscess model. No clinical use or human trial result appears in any cited source.
purpose: Built to predict molecules that inhibit bacterial growth and surface antibiotic candidates. Halicin was that purpose.
system: Directed-message-passing neural network (D-MPNN) for antibacterial activity prediction (Chemprop-style, MIT)
developer: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Collins and Barzilay laboratories) with the Broad Institute
deployer: MIT / Broad Institute / McMaster University research teams

ratings.reason: The sources document in vitro and murine results and independent laboratory confirmation. No individually attributable real-world outcome such as a treated patient or an approved drug.

ai_role.statement: The neural network's prediction selected halicin for testing from compounds not previously recognized as antibiotics. Wet-lab experiments by the authors and later by independent groups confirmed the activity. The outcome so far is a laboratory and animal-model result.

produced_by: A growth-inhibition training set of a few thousand molecules
A message-passing network ranking large chemical libraries

must_hold: Predicted compounds must be available for synthesis or purchase

echoes.setting: Abaucin, a narrow-spectrum anti-Acinetobacter baumannii compound identified by a neural network trained on about 7,500 screened molecules (McMaster and MIT), controlled infection in a mouse wound model; preclinical only

headline: MIT neural network finds halicin, active in vitro and in mice

comparator.against: vehicle control and the first-line antibiotic metronidazole in a mouse Clostridioides difficile infection model
comparator.before: vehicle or the antibiotic metronidazole (lower clearance rate)
comparator.after: sterilization of 3 out of 4 mice after 72 hr of treatment, and 4 out of 4 mice after 96 hr of treatment
comparator.quote: Excitingly, we observed that halicin resulted in C. difficile clearance at a greater rate than vehicle or the antibiotic metronidazole (Figure 5F), which is not only a first-line treatment for C. difficile infection, but also the antibiotic most similar to halicin based on Tanimoto score (Figure 2H, Table S2H). Indeed, halicin resulted in sterilization of 3 out of 4 mice after 72 hr of treatment, and 4 out of 4 mice after 96 hr of treatment.

later.note: An independent laboratory at KACST in Riyadh confirmed halicin's in vitro activity against gram-positive and gram-negative strains, including a multidrug-resistant A. baumannii isolate; the compound remains preclinical.
later.quote: The new antibacterial agent was able to inhibit all tested gram-positive and gram-negative bacterial strains, but in different concentrations—including the A. baumannii multidrug-resistant (MDR) isolate.

fields.account: Jonathan Stokes, Regina Barzilay, James Collins and colleagues at MIT, the Broad Institute, Harvard and McMaster University published in Cell on 20 February 2020. They reported halicin, a molecule identified by a directed-message-passing neural network trained on 2,335 molecules to predict inhibition of E. coli growth. Halicin, originally investigated as a kinase inhibitor for diabetes, is structurally divergent from conventional antibiotics. It reduced Acinetobacter baumannii in a mouse wound model and cleared Clostridioides difficile in a mouse infection model. Independent laboratories at KACST in Riyadh (December 2021) and Central South University in Changsha (September 2022) confirmed antibacterial activity in vitro. The latter also in a mouse abscess model. No clinical use or human trial result appears in any cited source.
